target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove major scheduling barriers and make voting easier for everyone.
objection: Declaring Election Day a federal holiday would not reliably solve the scheduling problem because federal law does not require private employers to give paid time off or close. Many workers in retail, food service, hospitals, and similar jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not guarantee time to vote.

target: AG1’s assumption that an Election Day holiday would broadly help voters rather than create new burdens.
objection: A holiday could disadvantage low-income workers: salaried or unionized employees may benefit from existing holiday policies, while hourly workers may still have to work or may lose pay if they are given unpaid time off. So the policy may help some people more than others and can leave the lowest-income workers no better off.

target: AG1’s implication that a holiday is the best or most reliable way to improve voting access.
objection: State-level reforms that directly require employer accommodations for voting, such as guaranteed time off or paid leave, are more dependable than merely making Election Day a holiday because they directly address the work-schedule barrier.

target: AG1’s broader claim that an election holiday is an effective turnout reform.
objection: Research suggests that simply declaring an election holiday is less effective at increasing turnout than targeted access measures such as guaranteed time to vote, expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday changes the default scheduling environment enough to solve the problem.
objection: The core problem is low-wage, hourly, customer-facing workers who are least able to take time off and whose workplaces often do not close on holidays. A holiday label does not require those employers to stop operations or provide paid time, so the key barrier remains for the workers most in need of help.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday reduces barriers by shifting the day into a more supportive environment for families and workers.
objection: The holiday can shift the burden onto low-income workers by creating unpaid time-off risks and lost wages, meaning it may reduce barriers for some while leaving the most vulnerable workers in essentially the same position or worse.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a national holiday creates a consistent baseline for access.
objection: A calendar change is mostly symbolic unless it comes with a legal requirement for paid or job-protected time to vote. A rule that directly mandates voting time is more consistent and more likely to benefit low-income workers than simply changing the holiday status.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday improves logistics such as childcare and weekday routines.
objection: That argument can cut the other way: low-cost childcare tied to school schedules may close or reduce hours on holidays, and essential retail/service workers still have to work. As a result, low-income families may face higher childcare costs or no workable coverage.

target: AG1’s position that a holiday is useful as a complement to other reforms.
objection: If the country still needs paid or job-protected time off and other concrete access reforms to ensure low-income workers can vote, then making Election Day a national holiday is largely redundant and risks being misleading as a centerpiece policy.

target: AG1’s view that a holiday meaningfully changes incentives even without forcing employers to close or pay holiday wages.
objection: Because private employers are not required to close or provide holiday pay, many hourly workers would still face the same wage tradeoff or the loss of hours. In practice, people whose employers already offer holiday time would benefit more, so the policy does not reliably target the biggest turnout barriers for low-income voters.
